messages.author: 91d53d643859f8d6
messages.subject: Approximating integer-valued latent variable
parts:
Hi Folks - 

I'm hoping to use Stan to estimate a model in which I would historically have included an integer-valued latent variable, and was wondering if the approach I'm hoping to use would break the gradient for HMC sufficiently to make it more worthwhile to use a sampler that explicitly deals with integer-valued latent variables.

So, I have a dataset on pediatric hospital admissions from 3 large hospitals and am trying to estimate age-specific rates of diarrheal disease risk for children < 5 years old as a function of social and environmental covariates. I'm hoping to model the counts for each age/week using a Poisson log-linear model.

Unfortunately, one of the hospitals in my dataset only reported the year of birth for each child rather than their exact birthday or age at the date of admission. This means that each child has two possible ages, a_0 < a_1. We can model p(a_1 | year_birth, date_admission) as a bernoulli random variable, with success probability equal to the proportion of a full year elapsed between the date of admission in the year of birth and the end of the year. 

If I were hand-coding this, I would use a Gibbs step to marginalize out the latent vars and get on with life, but I'm hoping to take advantage of the HMC in stan to efficiently incorporate some spatial random effects. Marginalizing these using the approach described in the Stan manual, i.e explicitly writing the mixture probabilities, isn't really feasible because there are many individuals with partially observed birthdays (~ 20K), making calculation of the possible counts and mixture weights prohibitively expensive.

An alternative approach would be to treat the birthday as a uniformly distributed RV on the range from [Jan1, Dec31] in the year of birth, and then to count the individual as a_0 if the estimated date of birth occurs after the date of admission in the birth year and a_1 otherwise. 

This is of course not strictly kosher as far as Stan's sampler is concerned, but I was wondering if anyone had insight about whether this would interfere with the accurate estimation of the model and whether I would still get the benefits of HMC for the other truly continuous parameters. Any ideas/suggestions would be greatly appreciated!


Thanks!

-Jon Zelner

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Approximating integer-valued latent variable
parts:
Andrew's suggested tricks like that for dealign with discrete vars,
and I think the jury's still out as to whether they'll work at
larger scales than toy problems.

A discretized age seems like a bad predictor in pediatrics anyway,
as it's already very discontinuous and groups kids 364 days apart
in the same bin and separates kids 2 days apart into different bins.

Can you just make everything continuous and latent?

Also, the marginalization won't necessarily be so bad if there
are only two ages because the contribution to the likelihood is
probably on a per child basis. So there'd only be two terms for
each of the kids with a missing age. That'd probably be faster
than doing Gibbs on the variable anyway, but admittedly a pain
to write.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Approximating integer-valued latent variable
parts:
Couldn’t you model the binned kids (won’t you donate and help
a child who had been histogrammed?) as binned_year + delta,
where delta is a continuous latent parameter between [0, 365]?
You could even assign a prior to delta based on known birth
rates from census data.
